doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Leaving John Lewis and touring with Philly Joe Jones
summary: Cutting ties with Lewis and joining Philly Joe Jones despite warnings; Philly Joe's personality.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: But John was like a benevolent dictator. We used to have some battles. See now I got — I don’t know if it’s on the record or off the record but I guess I could say this, like every mentor you come to a point where you have to cut the ties. Because he really had me Svengali — I’m glad he did because I learned a lot but there comes a point where you’ve got to say hold it, I’ve got to find me. Which I think I have. In the 60s, oh yeah, I went on the road with Philly Joe Jones.
That must have been an experience.
Talk about a forceful personality. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

He — you know he was not just a gifted drummer, he could have been an actor, comedian, he used to do these — he was obsessed with Bela Lugosi and he used to do all these imitations, his voice and everything, and do all the routines from the movies. He made a record called “Dracula” of Philly Joe Jones and Dracula.

Yeah. Of course he owes me money like he owes everybody else money. He had his drug thing. I think he beat it, or at least — I never was clear if he actually really beat it forever. I don’t know if he ever went back. But John warned me about — John got very angry with me because I was going to go join him. He said, “You can’t do that, he’s a gangster, you don’t know those people.” He was like a father, he was saying you’re nuts, you can’t do that. I said I’m going, I went. It wasn’t that long, a couple of months or whatever it was. And it was quite an experience.
